# Jeremiah 20: Verse-by-Verse Research Notes

**Before you use these notes:**
- The search budget ran out, so some sources never came up: bibleodyssey.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org, Lutheran sites and the Pentecostal journals. Catholic material comes from Haydock's commentary on studylight. The NET notes are as quoted on preceptaustin.
- The preceptaustin page I opened was cut off partway through v. 3. Its points on later verses come from search snippets.
- I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching about this chapter, so that topic is left out.
- In what I read, the Protestant traditions don't split into clear camps. They differ mostly in tone, and only at v. 7 and v. 14.

---

**v. 1**
- Pashhur ran the temple and could control what happened in its courts. What set him off was Jeremiah's message of judgment in chapter 19. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-20-commentary
- NET note: his job was keeping order in the temple, a post second only to the high priest. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-20-commentary
- Calvin: Pashhur's guilt was worse because he struck God's servant, a long-serving prophet, not an ordinary person. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/20-1.html
- Matthew Henry: the process was illegal. Jeremiah's credentials should have been examined before he was punished. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_020.cfm
- Catholic (Haydock): Pashhur's duty was to arrest impostors, and he treated Jeremiah as one. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/jeremiah-20.html

**v. 2**
- Guzik, quoting Morgan: "smote" is probably a technical term for the official 39 lashes. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-20/
- Harrison and Kidner: the word for "stocks" comes from a root meaning "to twist." The frame held prisoners in a cramped, painful position. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-20/
- Feinberg: the Upper Benjamin Gate was one of the most public places in the city. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-20/
- NET note: this gate was probably the north gate of the temple's inner court, not the city-wall gate of the same name. The meaning of "stocks" is uncertain. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-20-commentary
- Utley: God had promised to protect Jeremiah (1:18–19), but that did not mean he would escape suffering. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-20-commentary

**v. 3**
- Guzik: Pashhur may have thought releasing Jeremiah was kind. The old name was taken to mean "freedom" or "ease"; Magor-missabib means "terror on every side." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-20/
- Preceptaustin: the new name is a declaration, a living prophecy of the Babylonian invasion. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-20-commentary
- Catholic (Challoner, in Haydock): the name was changed to show the punishment coming for opposing God's word. Haydock also lists other ancient readings of the name. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/jeremiah-20.html

**v. 4**
- Guzik: Jeremiah did not soften his message, and Pashhur would be at the centre of the destruction. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-20/
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the terror would grow out of Pashhur's own false prophecies, and the "friends" are those who believed them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/jeremiah-20.html
- Matthew Henry: God does not strike him dead but lets him live in constant fear, like Cain. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_020.cfm

**v. 5**
- Guzik: the message is the same as before. Neither God nor Egypt would rescue Judah, and Babylon would conquer it completely. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-20/
- Matthew Henry: silencing the preacher gains nothing, because the word will run its course anyway. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_020.cfm

**v. 6**
- Guzik: his rank would not protect Pashhur. He "prophesied lies" and would die in Babylon. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-20/
- Matthew Henry: Pashhur opposed Jeremiah because Jeremiah's message threatened to wake people he was lulling to sleep in their sins. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_020.cfm
- Catholic (Calmet, in Haydock): this verse shows Pashhur was a false prophet. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/jeremiah-20.html

**v. 7** (the most debated verse)
- **Traditional reading:**
  - Ellicott: the story ends here and a psalm of complaint begins, likely Jeremiah's thoughts on his night of shame. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/20-7.htm
  - Benson: "deceived" is a harsh rendering. The words properly mean "Thou hast persuaded me, and I was persuaded." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/20-7.htm
  - Pulpit Commentary: the sense is "entice." Jeremiah means his early reluctance to accept the call in chapter 1. https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/20-7.htm
  - Barnes: Jeremiah may have taken the promise in 1:18 too literally, as a pledge that he would succeed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/20-7.html
  - Feinberg (in Coffman): the verb is used of seducing a virgin (Ex 22:16). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/20-7.html
  - Guzik, quoting Thompson: Jeremiah felt his bond with God was like a marriage, yet he had been enticed, used and set aside. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-20/
  - BibleHub Study Bible: this is raw emotion, not a claim that God lies. https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/20-7.htm
- **Where traditions differ:**
  - Reformed: Calvin reads the words as ironic. Jeremiah is repeating his enemies' charge that he is an impostor, to show they were really insulting God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/20-7.html
  - Reformed: the Geneva Bible instead sees here the impatience that overcomes God's servants when their work bears no fruit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/20-7.htm
  - Baptist: Gill cites Luther's rendering, "Thou hast persuaded me." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/20-7.htm
  - Baptist: Gill also sees in the passage a mixture of grace and corruption, flesh struggling against spirit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/20-7.htm
  - Matthew Henry: it was Jeremiah's weakness to complain this way. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_020.cfm
- **Catholic:**
  - Challoner (in Haydock): the "deceiving" was only God not telling Jeremiah, at his call, how much he would suffer. God never promised him freedom from persecution. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/jeremiah-20.html
  - The Catholic New American Bible translates it "You seduced me." https://biblehub.com/catholic/jeremiah/20-7.htm
- **Modern translation:** the NET Bible says God "coerced me into being a prophet." https://biblehub.com/lexicon/jeremiah/20-7.htm

**v. 8**
- Barnes: from the start of his ministry Jeremiah had reason only to lament. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/20-8.htm
- Matthew Henry: Jeremiah condemned the people's violence and also foretold violence coming on them. They mocked him as too strict for the first and too gullible for the second. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_020.cfm
- Harrison: people laughed at him because his predictions went unfulfilled for so long. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-20/
- Catholic (Menochius, in Haydock): Jeremiah was guilty of a "venial" (minor) faintheartedness here. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/jeremiah-20.html

**v. 9**
- Morgan (in Guzik): silence became more unbearable than suffering. He links this to Paul's "Woe is me if I preach not the gospel." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-20/
- Cundall (in Guzik): Jeremiah voiced his doubts only to God, never in public. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-20/
- Feinberg: the call could not be reversed and God's word could not be held down. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-20-commentary
- Geneva Bible: he would have stopped preaching if God's Spirit had not compelled him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/20-8.htm
- Catholic (Haydock): compare Acts 17:16 and 1 Corinthians 9:16. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/jeremiah-20.html

**v. 10**
- Barnes:
  - The "whispering" is people plotting in small groups.
  - "Report him" means they urged each other to inform against him.
  - "My trusted friends" is literally "men of my peace," meaning acquaintances.
  - "Deceived" is the same verb as in v. 7.
  https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nlt/jeremiah/20-14.html
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: they meant to report him to the Sanhedrin. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/jeremiah-20.html
- Harrison: "Terror on every side" may have been a mocking nickname for Jeremiah himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-20/
- Catholic (Calmet): his enemies watched for a chance to ruin him, as the Pharisees did with Jesus. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/jeremiah-20.html

**v. 11**
- Guzik: as God's greatness came into focus, Jeremiah's misery shrank. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-20/
- Ellicott: "not prosper" is better read as "have not dealt wisely." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/20-11.htm
- Keil and Delitzsch: Jeremiah calls God a warrior because God promised to rescue him from violent men. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/20-11.htm
- Mackay: the persecutors' disgrace will be permanent. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-20-commentary

**v. 12**
- Matthew Henry: God, who sees the heart, is the right judge of both the righteous and the wicked. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_020.cfm
- BibleHub: the lesson is to seek God's justice rather than take revenge yourself. https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/20.htm
- Catholic (Challoner): this prayer came from zeal for justice, not from hatred. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/jeremiah-20.html

**v. 13**
- Guzik: his troubles were not over, yet he was confident of God's victory. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-20/
- BibleHub: rescuing "the needy" points ahead to Jesus' mission statement in Luke 4:18. https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/20.htm
- Catholic (Theodoret): his thanksgiving shows that what follows in vv. 14–18 does not come from impatience. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/jeremiah-20.html

**v. 14** (why the sudden switch from praise to curse, and was it sin?)
- **Placement:**
  - Calvin, followed by Grotius and Henry: Jeremiah is recalling what he felt earlier, in the stocks. https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom19/calcom19.iii.xvii.html
  - Methodist: Wesley says some take these words as Jeremiah repeating an earlier outburst. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-jeremiah/
  - Clarke: these verses belong after v. 8. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/niv/jeremiah/20-14.html
  - Ewald wanted to move vv. 14–18 before vv. 7–12. Keil disagreed: these may be separate struggles at different times. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/20-14.htm
- **Was it sin? Views differ:**
  - Reformed: Calvin says the prophet sinned grievously. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/20-14.html
  - Baptist: Gill calls it impatience, weak faith and folly. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/20-14.htm
  - Barnes: impatience is the most blameworthy part of Jeremiah's character. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nlt/jeremiah/20-14.html
  - Lowth (cited by Benson): these words express mourning, not malice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/20-14.htm
  - BibleHub Study Bible: God does not rebuke Jeremiah here. https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/20-14.htm
  - Catholic (Challoner): it is a figure of speech showing how great his sufferings were. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/jeremiah-20.html
- **Modern scholarship:**
  - Expositor's Bible: the passage carries no formula claiming divine inspiration; it records Jeremiah's own feelings. It suggests the author of Job may have built on these verses. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/ubv/jeremiah/20-14.html
  - Ellicott takes the opposite view: Jeremiah borrowed from Job. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/20-14.htm

**v. 15**
- Coffman and Constable: cursing one's parents was a capital crime, so Jeremiah carefully curses the day and the messenger instead. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/20-14.html

**v. 16**
- The "cities" are Sodom and Gomorrah. The cries are the shouts of enemies breaking in. Wesley: https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-jeremiah/ and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/jeremiah-20.html
- Calmet: being alarmed at noon is stranger than at night, so he means constant terror. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/jeremiah-20.html

**v. 17**
- Catholic (Haydock): the Septuagint (ancient Greek translation) reads "because he [the Lord] slew me not." Jerome: it is better not to exist than to live in constant misery. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/jeremiah-20.html

**v. 18**
- Preceptaustin: Jeremiah is wrestling with the purpose of his life. Like Job, he grieves to God rather than turning away from Him. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah-20-commentary
- Keil and Delitzsch: unlike Job, Jeremiah never directly blames God for giving him life. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/20-15.html
- Guzik: faith did not remove his struggle; it required constant dependence on God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-20/
